title: Social context and women who find services hard to reach
blurb: Recognise complex social factors, treat late booking as a signal, and adapt care with other agencies so every woman can reach it.
question: Mariam, 24, an asylum seeker who speaks Tigrinya, has her first maternity contact at 23 weeks after being moved to a new hostel. How should the midwife respond to her late booking and adapt her care?

teach.h: Services that are hard to reach
teach.body: Formally, NICE CG110 names complex social factors in pregnancy: poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, recent arrival as a migrant, asylum seeker or refugee status, difficulty speaking or understanding English, age under 20 and domestic abuse. In plain English: some women do not 'fail to engage'; the service is hard for them to reach. Midwives must understand women's lives and adapt care, working with other agencies (SPM 2.7-2.9).

teach.caption: Recent migrant = moved to the UK within the previous 12 months. Factors vary in type and prevalence between local populations.

teach.h: Late booking is a warning sign
teach.body: NICE expects booking by 10+0 weeks (NG201 1.1.4). If a woman books later, ask about her reasons (NG201 1.1.6), without judgement. If she has no booking at first contact with any professional, discuss the need for antenatal care and offer booking, or referral to sexual health services if she is considering termination (CG110 1.1.11). Late booking can signal an abusive partner preventing attendance, unfamiliarity with the NHS, or fear of children's services (CG110).

head: Group
Key adaptations
rows: Refer at first disclosure; named specialist midwife or doctor; text reminders; transport help
Professional interpreter; longer appointments; info on entitlement; keep notes with her
Named midwife; community, age-appropriate care; peer groups; transport help
Named midwife; flexible visits; confidential record; helpline card

teach.h: From first contact to coordinated care
teach.caption: CG110 1.1.7: consider a multi-agency needs assessment so the woman has one coordinated care plan.

teach.body: Midwife Ellen books Mariam at the first contact, using a professional Tigrinya interpreter rather than a fellow resident (CG110 1.3.10), and allows a longer appointment (1.3.4). She asks gently why care started late, gives information on access and entitlement (1.3.7), asks Mariam to keep her hand-held notes with her at all times (1.3.8) and to report address changes, and liaises with the hostel's housing team to keep contact details current (1.3.3).

teach.text: Do not interpret missed appointments as lack of interest. CG110 asks services to remove barriers: transport help, text reminders, flexible and longer appointments, and care in community settings. And avoid assumptions based on a woman's culture, ethnic origin or religion (CG110 1.3.9).

items: CG110 complex social factors: poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, migrants, asylum seekers and refugees, language barriers, under 20, domestic abuse.
Book at first contact, ask why booking was late, and remove barriers rather than discharging.
Professional interpreters, longer appointments and information on entitlement for migrant women.
Named midwife for under 20s and women experiencing abuse; named specialist for substance misuse.
Coordinate a multi-agency plan, including safeguarding, and keep contact details current.

summary: You can now identify complex social factors and the barriers they create, respond to late booking as a warning sign, and adapt care for migrant, young, substance-using and abused women. You can also coordinate a multi-agency plan around a woman's social context.

A.q: Zoe first contacts maternity services at 20 weeks of pregnancy. After offering a booking appointment, what does NICE NG201 recommend the midwife does about the late booking?
options: Remind her that booking should happen by 10 weeks
Refer her to obstetric-led care because she is late
Ask about her reasons for booking late, without judgement
Delay booking until her next routine appointment
A.why: NG201 1.1.6: ask women who book late about their reasons. Late booking can signal social complexity or safeguarding concerns.

whyNot.0: A reminder does not identify the barrier and may feel judgemental.
whyNot.1: Late booking alone is not an indication for obstetric-led care.
whyNot.3: CG110 1.1.11 says offer booking at first contact, not later.

A.q: In NICE CG110, how is a 'recent migrant' defined?
options: A woman who moved to the UK within the previous 12 months
A woman who moved to the UK within the previous 6 months
A woman who moved to the UK within the previous 2 years
A woman who moved to the UK within the previous 5 years
A.why: CG110 defines recent migrants as women who moved to the UK within the previous 12 months.

whyNot.1: Six months is shorter than the CG110 definition.
whyNot.2: Two years is longer than the CG110 definition.
whyNot.3: Five years is far longer than the CG110 definition.

A.q: Mariam speaks Tigrinya and little English. Another resident from her hostel offers to interpret at booking. What should the midwife arrange?
options: Accept the resident, as they share a language
Use translated leaflets without interpreting
Ask Mariam's partner to interpret for her
Use a professional interpreter instead
A.why: CG110 1.3.10: provide an interpreter (who may be a link worker or advocate) who communicates in her preferred language and is not her partner or family; a fellow resident is not independent or bound by confidentiality.

whyNot.0: A fellow resident is not an independent, confidential interpreter.
whyNot.1: Leaflets help but do not allow a two-way booking conversation.

B.q: Kayla, 22, tells the midwife at her first appointment that she uses heroin daily. What does NICE CG110 recommend at this first disclosure?
options: Wait until after the anomaly scan before referring
Advise her to stop using before the next visit
Offer referral to a substance misuse programme
Refer to children's social care before booking
B.why: CG110 1.2.7: the first time a woman who misuses substances discloses that she is pregnant, offer referral to an appropriate substance misuse programme.

whyNot.0: NICE says to offer referral at the first disclosure, not later.
whyNot.1: Sudden cessation advice without support is not the NICE recommendation.
whyNot.3: Safeguarding may be considered, but booking and referral to treatment should not be delayed.

B.q: Mariam may be moved between asylum accommodation during her pregnancy. Which action best maintains her care?
options: Keep her notes in the hospital so they are not lost
Discharge her if she moves out of the local area
Advise her to keep her hand-held notes with her
Send her letters to the address on her booking
B.why: CG110 1.3.8: discuss the importance of keeping her hand-held maternity record with her at all times; 1.1.5 lets women take a copy when they move.

whyNot.0: Notes held in hospital do not travel with her if she moves.
whyNot.1: Discharge on moving breaks her care; services should help her transfer.
whyNot.3: Her address may change; CG110 1.3.3 asks staff to work with housing agencies to keep details current.

B.q: Rachel discloses domestic abuse at 30 weeks. Alongside other support, what does CG110 recommend the midwife gives her?
options: A full printed copy of her confidential notes
A credit card-sized card with helpline numbers
A letter for her partner explaining the referral
A leaflet about the risks of abuse in pregnancy
B.why: CG110 1.5.10: give the woman a credit card-sized information card that includes local and national helpline numbers, easy to conceal.

whyNot.0: Taking home confidential notes could be found by the abuser.
whyNot.2: Writing to the partner could put her at risk.
whyNot.3: A leaflet is larger and easier to find; CG110 specifies a small card.

C.q: Jess, 16, has missed two appointments. She says the hospital clinic is full of older women, she feels embarrassed and the bus is expensive. What is the most appropriate plan?
options: Discharge her to the GP after the second missed visit
Ask her parents to make sure she attends every visit
Refer her to the hospital consultant clinic for review
Offer community care, a named midwife and travel help
C.why: CG110 1.4.1 and 1.4.4: offer age-appropriate, community-based care, help with transport and a named midwife who provides most of her care.

whyNot.0: Discharge abandons a young woman CG110 asks services to reach out to.
whyNot.1: Involving parents without her agreement may breach confidentiality and does not remove barriers.
whyNot.2: A hospital clinic is the barrier she describes.

C.q: Kayla, 22, is homeless, uses heroin and is 18 weeks pregnant. Several agencies are involved but none share a plan. What should the midwife consider first?
options: A multi-agency needs assessment and one coordinated plan
Leaving coordination to the substance misuse service
Extra hospital scans to monitor the baby's growth
Discussing her case at the next antenatal team meeting
C.why: CG110 1.1.7 and 1.2.3: consider a multi-agency needs assessment, including safeguarding, so the woman has a coordinated care plan, with notes combined into a single document.

whyNot.1: No single agency should hold coordination alone; the midwife coordinates maternity care within the plan.
whyNot.2: Scans may be needed but do not address the fragmented care.
whyNot.3: An internal meeting does not join up the agencies involved.

C.q: A local maternity system uses NHS England's Core20PLUS5 approach to target continuity teams. Who are the 'Core20'?
options: The 20% of women with the most complex needs
The most deprived 20% of the national population
The 20 most deprived local authorities in England
The 20% of women who book after 20 weeks
C.why: Core20 is the most deprived 20% of the national population as identified by the Index of Multiple Deprivation.

whyNot.0: Complexity of need is not how the Core20 is defined.
whyNot.2: The definition uses population deprivation, not a list of authorities.
whyNot.3: Late booking is not the Core20 definition.

reteach.title: Move the service, not the woman
reteach.question: If a woman keeps missing appointments, what might be getting in her way, and what can the service change?

blocks.body: Cost of travel, fear of authorities, an abusive partner, language, shame at being young or using drugs, and moving address all keep women from care. NICE asks services to change: named midwives, community clinics, interpreters, longer slots, reminders, transport help and joined-up plans with housing, substance and abuse services.

blocks.text: 'Did not attend' is a prompt to ask why and adapt, not a reason to discharge.

explain.body: Midwives apply knowledge of the social context in which women live (SPM 2.7), reach out to women who find services difficult to access (2.8) and work with other agencies on the social determinants of health (2.9). CG110 lists the complex social factors.

test.q: Which of these is listed as a complex social factor in NICE CG110?
options: Age 35 or over
First pregnancy
Age under 20
Previous caesarean
test.why: CG110 names age under 20 alongside poverty, homelessness, substance misuse, migration, language and domestic abuse.

whyNot.0: Age 35 or over is a clinical risk factor, not a CG110 social factor.
whyNot.1: Nulliparity is not a social factor.
whyNot.3: Previous caesarean is an obstetric factor.

explain.body: Book by 10+0 weeks; ask about reasons for late booking; offer booking at first contact with any professional; give a phone number for address changes and an out-of-hours number (CG110 1.1.11-1.1.13).

test.q: At booking, what does CG110 recommend giving every woman with complex social factors so she can get help outside normal hours?
options: A number for triage or the labour ward
The GP surgery's main number
A national pregnancy helpline
Her community midwife's home number
test.why: CG110 1.1.13: give a telephone number to contact a healthcare professional out of hours, for example hospital triage, the labour ward or the birth centre.

whyNot.1: GP surgeries are usually closed out of hours.
whyNot.2: A general helpline is not a direct route to her maternity team.
whyNot.3: Personal home numbers are not appropriate or reliable.

explain.body: Use a variety of communication methods; train staff in migrant women's needs (including FGM and HIV); provide professional interpreters, not partners or family; allow longer appointments; give information on access and entitlement; check understanding (CG110 1.3).

test.q: When a professional interpreter is used at antenatal visits, what does CG110 say services should offer?
options: Fewer, shorter appointments
Group appointments with others
Appointments by telephone
More flexible, longer appointments
test.why: CG110 1.3.4: offer flexibility in the number and length of appointments when interpreting services are used.

whyNot.0: Interpreting takes more time, not less.
whyNot.1: Group sessions reduce privacy for sensitive questions.
whyNot.2: Telephone appointments are not what CG110 recommends here.

explain.body: Under 20s: age-appropriate community care, peer groups, transport help, partner involvement with her agreement, named midwife (CG110 1.4). Domestic abuse: flexible appointments, named midwife, confidential record, helpline card, referral to a support worker (1.5).

test.q: According to CG110, when should the partner of a young woman under 20 be involved in her antenatal care?
options: At every appointment
With her agreement
Once she reaches 18
When the GP advises it
test.why: CG110 1.4.1: provide opportunities for the partner or father of the baby to be involved, with her agreement.

whyNot.0: Routine involvement without her agreement removes her control.
whyNot.2: CG110 does not set an age for partner involvement.
whyNot.3: The decision is hers, not the GP's.
